topic_title: Settlements (rural and urban) and service provision
topic: 1.5 Settlements (rural and urban) and service provision

items.prompt: Describe the difference between a nucleated settlement pattern and a dispersed settlement pattern.
items.canonical_answer: Nucleated means the buildings are clustered together round a centre, such as a church, a well or a market square, so the settlement occupies one compact patch of ground. Dispersed means the buildings are spread out across the land, each homestead standing alone on the ground it works, as farmsteads do on large commercial farms.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, 2 in all: clustered round a centre for nucleated; spread out across the land for dispersed.
Each feature names the shape the buildings make, which is what the question asks about.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.5 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Explain the patterns of settlement

items.prompt: Explain why settlement in dry country often follows a linear pattern along a river.
items.canonical_answer: Because the river is where the water is, houses string along its banks so that every household is within reach of water in a land where rain is unreliable. The valley floor also gives flat, deep-soiled land that is easier to build and farm than the slopes above it, and the river doubles as a route, so a line of settlement gains transport as well as water. Because the dry ground away from the river offers none of these, the settlement hugs the line rather than spreading out, so the pattern is linear.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3, each point a because-and-so step: water within reach along the banks; flat valley-floor land for building and farming; the river as a route, so the settlement spreads along the line rather than outwards.

items.prompt:
The sketch grid below shows part of a commercial farming area in central Namibia. Each cell is one square kilometre, with eastings 18 to 22 across and northings 40 to 42 down.

| northing | E18 | E19 | E20 | E21 | E22 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| N42 | grazing land | grazing land | grazing land | grazing land | grazing land |
| N41 | grazing land | farmstead and borehole | grazing land | grazing land | grazing land |
| N40 | grazing land | farmstead and borehole | farmstead and borehole | grazing land | grazing land |

Describe the settlement pattern shown on the grid.
items.canonical_answer: The grid shows a dispersed pattern: three farmsteads stand on the fifteen square kilometres shown, each on its own borehole and kilometres from the next, so the homesteads are spread across the farmland rather than gathered anywhere. The map shows no cluster of buildings at a single point, so the pattern is not nucleated, and the farmsteads sit beside two different eastings rather than stringing along one road or valley, so the values point away from linear too: the pattern shown is isolated homesteads on their own ground, which means dispersed.
marking_guidance: Reading: the pattern read from the grid, three isolated farmsteads with no cluster and no line (1 mark).

Values: the figures used, 3 farmsteads across 15 square kilometres, each on its own borehole (1 mark); so the answer rules out nucleated and linear in turn, which means the figures support the conclusion (1 mark).

items.prompt: Looking at a map on which twenty farmhouses stand strung along one straight valley road, a learner writes: 'This is a nucleated pattern because the houses are close together.' Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: Nucleated means buildings clustered round a centre in a compact group, whereas the map shows houses strung in a line along the road, which is a linear pattern. The error is reading closeness along a line as clustering round a point; the test is the shape the buildings make on the map, and here that shape is a strung-out line, not a cluster, so the pattern is linear.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named, a line of houses mistaken for a cluster; a nucleated settlement groups round a centre.
1 mark: the correct idea, buildings strung along a road are linear, which is not the same shape as clustered round a point.

items.prompt: In a scattered farming area, the council proposes closing the scattered farm schools and building one large primary school in the village at the area's centre, where 250 of the area's 900 children already live. Suggest how far this is a good decision.
items.canonical_answer: The judgement is that the plan is partly good, because it trades travel for quality. For: one central school with 900 children can support specialist teachers, a library and a hall, which scattered schools of 30 or 40 pupils cannot, and the 250 children living in the village would find their school at their doorstep. Against: the other 650 children face longer daily journeys on gravel roads, so some may attend less often, and the plan removes the service from the dispersed pattern the area's settlement has always had. On the evidence, the plan is justified provided transport is organised, because the gain in teaching quality is certain while the cost is travel time, not lost schooling.
marking_guidance: Judgement: 1 mark for a stated decision, partly good, because the quality gains are certain and the travel cost can be managed.
Because: 1 mark for the reasoning weighed, specialist teaching for 900 pupils against longer journeys for the 650 children outside the village.
Evidence: 1 mark for the figures used, 250 of 900 children in the village and schools of 30 to 40 pupils, so the judgement rests on data rather than opinion.

items.prompt: State what is meant by the site of a settlement.
items.canonical_answer: The land the settlement is built on and its physical features: its water supply, its relief, its soil, its building materials and, historically, its defensive value.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning of the term, the ground the settlement stands on with one physical feature of it; its position relative to other places is situation, not site.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.5 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and explain the factors which may influence the sites, growth and functions of settlements

items.prompt: Explain why the first settlements in an area usually began beside a reliable water supply and on flat land.
items.canonical_answer: Because a household needs water every day for drinking, cooking and livestock, a site beside a spring, river or well spared people the labour of carrying it far, so reliable water anchored the first settlement. Flat land, in turn, is cheaper and easier to build on than a slope, because foundations and tracks need less work, and flat, well-drained soil is usually the most fertile, so the same ground sheltered the people and fed them, which is how a good site earned its choice.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3, each point a because-and-so step: daily water needs met without long carrying; building is easier and cheaper on flat ground; so fertile flat soil also grows the food, which links the two site factors into one reason.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.5 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and explain the factors which may influence the sites, growth and functions of settlements

items.prompt: Asked for the reasons for a settlement's site, a learner writes: 'Okahandja's site is excellent because it stands on the main road north from Windhoek.' Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The learner has described Okahandja's situation, which is not the same as its site: situation is the settlement's position relative to the area around it, here the road that links the town to Windhoek. Site is the land the town is built on and its physical features, such as its water supply and the relief and soil of the ground itself, so an answer about the reasons for a site should come from the ground the town stands on, not from the roads around it.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named, the answer confuses site with situation, describing the surrounding road instead of the ground itself.
1 mark: the correct idea, site is the land the settlement is built on and its features, which is not the same as its position relative to the area around it.

items.prompt: Give the meaning of the term threshold population.
items.canonical_answer: The smallest number of people needed to keep a service in business: the customers a service must be able to draw on to survive, such as the population a hospital needs and a village shop does not.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning of the term, the minimum population a service needs to stay viable; accept its link to high-order and low-order services.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.5 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Give reasons for the hierarchy of settlements and services

items.prompt: Explain why a hospital is found in a large town while a village keeps no more than a clinic.
items.canonical_answer: A hospital is a high-order service: it needs specialist staff, equipment and wards, which cost a great deal, so it must draw on a threshold population of many tens of thousands to pay for itself. A village of a few hundred people cannot supply that, so the hospital sits in the large town, where the population is large and where patients from the whole sphere of influence can reach it, which is how the hierarchy places its services. The village keeps a clinic instead, because a clinic's threshold population is small and its work stays within reach of village life.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3: how a hospital's costs cause its large threshold population; so villages cannot support one, which places the hospital in the town; the clinic instead is a low-order service whose small threshold a village can meet.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.5 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Give reasons for the hierarchy of settlements and services

items.prompt:
The table shows five settlements of one district:

| settlement | population | number of services | highest-order service |
|---|---|---|---|
| Doorn | 320 | 3 | primary school |
| Riet | 4 800 | 11 | health centre |
| Klipbank | 21 000 | 34 | district hospital |
| Vley | 66 000 | 71 | university |
| Berg | 9 500 | 19 | secondary school |

Describe the relationship shown between settlement size and services.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows the settlement hierarchy at work: as population rises, so does the range of services, from Doorn's 3 services for 320 people to Vley's 71 services for 66 000. The order rises with it, because only Vley holds a university, the highest-order service listed, while Doorn's highest service is a primary school, and the values climb step by step between the two. The trend means Riet, fifteen times Doorn's size at 4 800 people, carries eleven services to its three, so a bigger settlement does not just add people: it adds higher-order services as well.
marking_guidance: Reading: the trend read from the table, more people, more services, in a step-by-step climb (1 mark).

Values: the figures quoted in support, such as 3 services at Doorn against 71 at Vley (1 mark); so the answer draws the meaning, the higher the population the higher the order of the top service, which is the hierarchy the table shows (1 mark).

items.prompt: The photograph shows a town's open market day in northern Namibia: hundreds of stalls under shade roofs, buyers who have come by pickup from villages up to 50 kilometres away, a clinic at the market's edge, and cattle pens beside the road. Suggest why the market stands in this town rather than in any of the villages around it.
items.canonical_answer: The market is a high-order service for the countryside around: a trader needs thousands of customers to make a day's sales worth the journey, and no single village holds that threshold population, so the market sits where the whole sphere of influence can gather, which is the town at the crossing of the routes the pickups use. The photograph suggests the reason: buyers travel up to 50 kilometres to it, which means the town serves a wide area no village can, and the clinic and cattle pens stand beside it because they draw their users from the same wide area too.
marking_guidance: Resource: the evidence used, buyers travelling up to 50 kilometres from the surrounding villages (1 mark).
Reasons: no village holds the market's threshold population, so the market sits in the town (1 mark); therefore the clinic and pens share the position, which the photograph here suggests (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.5 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Give reasons for the hierarchy of settlements and services

items.prompt: A learner writes: 'Windhoek is at the top of Namibia's settlement hierarchy because it covers the largest area.' Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The hierarchy ranks settlements by the number and order of their services, not by their physical size, so covering a large area of land is not the test: a spread-out settlement with few services would rank below a compact one with many. Windhoek does sit at the top, but in fact because it holds the country's main hospital, its university and its international airport, which are services of the highest order, not because of its area.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named, ranking by area instead of by the number and order of services.
1 mark: the correct idea, in fact Windhoek ranks top because of its highest-order services; the test of the ranking is whether it counts services.

items.prompt: A shoe shop can open in a village of 600 people or in a town of 40 000 people, 20 kilometres away, and the rent is the same in both. Suggest which the shop should choose, with reasons.
items.canonical_answer: The town is the better decision. A shoe shop sells rarely to each customer, because shoes are bought months or years apart, so it needs a large threshold population passing it, and 600 villagers cannot buy enough pairs to keep it in business, whereas 40 000 townspeople, plus shoppers from the villages around the town, can. The evidence is in the counts of potential customers, so the shop belongs where they gather, because a threshold is about the reach of the population, not about the rent.
marking_guidance: Judgement: 1 mark for the stated decision, the town of 40 000.
Because: 1 mark for the reasoning, a shoe shop's rare purchases need a large threshold population, so 600 people cannot sustain it.
Evidence: 1 mark for the figures used, 600 against 40 000, so the judgement is justified with data.

items.prompt: For the Oshana area of northern Namibia, describe two features of its settlements.
items.canonical_answer: The area holds three fast-growing towns close together, Oshakati with about 59 000 people (2023), Ongwediva with about 34 000 and Ondangwa with about 30 000, all within about 30 kilometres of one another. Around them lies one of the densest farmed landscapes in Namibia, a rural population of about 230 000 (2023) whose homesteads and small settlements fill the ground between the towns.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, 2 in all: the corridor of three towns with their populations; the dense rural settlement around them.
Each feature is a fact of the named area, Oshana, not a general point about settlements.

items.prompt: For the Oshana area of northern Namibia, explain why the largest town provides services the surrounding villages do not.
items.canonical_answer: Oshakati's about 59 000 people (2023) give it the threshold population for services a village cannot support, so this example shows the hierarchy working in one place. Its intermediate hospital needs tens of thousands of potential patients to pay for its staff and wards, so it stands in the town and draws them from across the north. Its open market needs the trade of the whole surrounding countryside, so traders and buyers gather there rather than in any village. Because the villages hold a few hundred people each, they keep a clinic, a primary school and small shops, which means villagers travel to Oshakati for anything high-order, and the town's place on the main road through the north makes that journey possible.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 4, each point from the named example: the hospital's threshold population explains its place in the town; the market draws the countryside's trade; so the villages keep only low-order services because their populations are small; therefore villagers travel up the hierarchy, because the road network makes the journey possible.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.5 claim ledger.
objective_titles: A case study of settlement and service provision in an area

items.prompt:
The table shows the towns of the Oshana corridor and their services (2023 census):

| town | population | hospital | open market | airport | secondary school |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Oshakati | 58 656 | yes | yes | no | yes |
| Ongwediva | 33 777 | no | no | no | yes |
| Ondangwa | 30 364 | no | no | yes | yes |

Describe the pattern of services shown.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows the towns sharing some services and dividing others. All three hold secondary schools, so schooling is spread across the corridor. But the high-order services divide: only Oshakati, the largest town at 58 656 people, holds a hospital, which means the two smaller towns' 64 000 people depend on Oshakati for hospital care, and only Ondangwa holds the airport. The pattern shown is a hierarchy within 30 kilometres: the values place the highest-order service in the largest town, so population size sorts the services.
marking_guidance: Reading: the pattern read from the table, shared schooling against divided high-order services (1 mark).

Values: the figures used, 58 656 for Oshakati with the hospital there against its absence in the smaller towns, and the 64 000 people served from it (1 mark); so the table shows the hierarchy at work in one small area, which means population sorts the services (1 mark).

items.prompt: For a named area you have studied, describe its settlements and services and explain why its largest town provides services the smaller settlements lack. [7]
items.canonical_answer: The Oshana region of northern Namibia holds three towns within about 30 kilometres of each other, Oshakati with about 59 000 people (2023), Ongwediva with about 34 000 and Ondangwa with about 30 000, surrounded by dense smallholder farmland of about 230 000 people. The services stack as the hierarchy predicts: every town holds secondary schools and banks, but only Oshakati holds the intermediate hospital and the large open market, and only Ondangwa holds the airport, while the villages keep a clinic, a primary school and small shops. The reason is threshold population. A hospital needs tens of thousands of potential patients to pay for its staff and wards, and only Oshakati's 59 000, drawing on the whole north, supplies that; a market needs thousands of buyers a day, which only the corridor's crossroads town gathers; a village of a few hundred supports a shop and a primary school and nothing above them, so its people travel up the hierarchy, by bus and pickup, for what their own settlement cannot pay for.
marking_guidance: Level 1 (1-3): simple statements about towns and villages, with no named example or only general points.
Level 2 (4-6): developed and linked statements about a named area, capped at 5 if no named example is given.

Level 3 (7): comprehensive statements with place-specific detail, Oshakati, Ongwediva and Ondangwa with their populations, the intermediate hospital, the airport at Ondangwa, covering the settlements, the services and the reasons.

A case study of settlement and service provision in an area

items.prompt:
Four settlements lie along one valley in a region. The table shows what each place holds:

| service | Sterk | Laagte | Pan | Fontein |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| population | 640 | 3 500 | 18 000 | 90 000 |
| primary school | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| clinic | no | yes | yes | yes |
| secondary school | no | no | yes | yes |
| hospital | no | no | no | yes |
| supermarket | no | no | yes | yes |

(a) Identify the settlement to which people from the whole region travel for hospital treatment. [1]
(b) Describe two differences between the services of Sterk and Pan. [2]
(c) Suggest why the secondary school is in Pan and not in Sterk. [3]
(d) Suggest why a new supermarket would open in Pan rather than in Laagte. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Fontein.
(b) Pan holds a secondary school, a clinic and a supermarket, while Sterk holds a primary school and no other service, so Sterk's children must travel out for secondary schooling and Sterk has no shop beyond a village store. Pan also serves a far larger population, 18 000 people against Sterk's 640.
(c) A secondary school needs several hundred pupils of secondary age to fill its classrooms and pay its teachers, so it needs a large threshold population. Sterk's 640 people cannot supply that, so a school there would run half-empty; Pan's 18 000 can, and the school also gathers children from Laagte and Sterk, who travel in. That is why the school sits in the settlement large enough to anchor it.
(d) A supermarket draws on a bigger spending pool than Laagte offers: 18 000 people against 3 500 means more customers every week, and Pan's position between the smaller settlements gives the shop a wider sphere of influence, so it opens where the custom is.
marking_guidance: Resource: (a) 1 mark for the settlement read from the table, Fontein, the one place with a hospital.
Marks and figures: (b) 2 marks, 1 per difference with the values from the table, Pan's secondary school, clinic and supermarket against Sterk's primary school alone.
Threshold: (c) 3 marks, the threshold population idea (1), the figures compared, 18 000 against 640 (1), and the consequence for Sterk's children, who travel to Pan (1).
Evidence: (d) 2 marks, 18 000 people against 3 500 as a market (1), so the data suggests more customers and a wider sphere of influence in Pan (1).
